system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Episodic ataxia type 2 due to CACNA1A dysfunction
mechanism: CACNA1A encodes the alpha-1A subunit of the presynaptic CaV2.1 P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channel. EA2 commonly results from loss-of-function variants that disturb cerebellar neurotransmission, causing hours-long attacks of ataxia/vertigo with interictal nystagmus and often response to acetazolamide.
vignette: A 16-year-old girl has recurrent attacks of vertigo, dysarthria, and severe gait ataxia lasting 4 to 8 hours. Episodes are triggered by strenuous exercise or emotional stress. Between attacks, examination shows gaze-evoked nystagmus but normal strength and sensation. Her father has similar episodes. Acetazolamide substantially reduces attack frequency.
lead: Dysfunction of which ion channel most likely causes this disorder?
correct: Presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels encoded by CACNA1A
distractors: Voltage-gated Kv1.1 potassium channels encoded by KCNA1
Skeletal-muscle chloride channels encoded by CLCN1
Ryanodine receptor calcium-release channels encoded by RYR1
Voltage-gated sodium channels encoded by SCN4A
distractor_notes: KCNA1 causes episodic ataxia type 1, which typically has much briefer attacks and interictal myokymia.
CLCN1 causes myotonia congenita, not a recurrent cerebellar syndrome.
RYR1 variants cause malignant hyperthermia and congenital myopathies rather than classic EA2.
SCN4A disorders primarily affect skeletal muscle excitability and do not explain interictal nystagmus with hours-long ataxia.
key_expl: EA2 is a CACNA1A channelopathy. CACNA1A encodes CaV2.1, the P/Q-type calcium-channel alpha-1A subunit that regulates neurotransmitter release and is highly important in cerebellar circuits.
objective: Associate hours-long episodic ataxia with interictal nystagmus and acetazolamide response with CACNA1A/P/Q-type calcium-channel dysfunction.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
diagnosis: Hereditary hyperekplexia due to GLRA1 dysfunction
mechanism: GLRA1 encodes the alpha-1 subunit of the inhibitory glycine receptor, a ligand-gated chloride channel concentrated in brainstem and spinal-cord circuits. Impaired glycinergic inhibition produces neonatal hypertonia and an exaggerated generalized startle response to unexpected stimuli.
vignette: A 2-month-old boy has recurrent episodes of sudden generalized stiffening after unexpected sounds or touch. He remains conscious during the episodes. Since birth he has had increased muscle tone, and tapping the bridge of the nose produces a reproducible generalized startle without habituation. EEG during an event shows no epileptiform activity. His father had similar symptoms as an infant.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains this patient's findings?
distractors: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome
Congenital myotonia
Stiff-person syndrome
Sandifer syndrome
distractor_notes: Epileptic spasms are associated with characteristic EEG abnormalities and are not specifically stimulus-triggered with preserved consciousness and nonhabituating nose-tap startle.
Congenital myotonia causes delayed muscle relaxation rather than an exaggerated brainstem startle reflex.
Stiff-person syndrome is an acquired autoimmune disorder, typically later in life, associated with axial rigidity and painful spasms.
Sandifer syndrome consists of dystonic posturing related to gastroesophageal reflux, not a reproducible generalized startle response.
key_expl: Hereditary hyperekplexia is a glycinergic inhibitory disorder. GLRA1 is the most common genetic cause; impaired inhibitory chloride-channel signaling in brainstem/spinal circuits causes neonatal stiffness and exaggerated startle while consciousness is preserved.
objective: Recognize hereditary hyperekplexia from neonatal hypertonia, preserved consciousness, stimulus-triggered nonhabituating startle, and normal EEG during events.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia due to PRRT2 dysfunction
mechanism: Heterozygous PRRT2 variants disturb presynaptic neurotransmitter release and cause brief paroxysmal dyskinesias triggered by sudden voluntary movement. Attacks usually last seconds to under a minute, consciousness is preserved, examination is normal between attacks, and carbamazepine often suppresses events.
vignette: A 14-year-old boy has dozens of daily episodes of sudden unilateral dystonic posturing and choreiform movements when he quickly rises from a chair or begins to run. Each episode lasts about 20 seconds. He remains fully conscious and has a normal neurologic examination between episodes. MRI and EEG are normal. His mother had similar attacks as a teenager. Low-dose carbamazepine nearly eliminates the episodes.
lead: Which cellular process is most likely disrupted by the gene responsible for this disorder?
correct: Presynaptic regulation of neurotransmitter release by PRRT2
distractors: Dopamine synthesis in substantia nigra neurons by tyrosine hydroxylase
GABA degradation by GABA transaminase
Acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction by botulinum-sensitive SNARE cleavage
Myelin compaction in central nervous system oligodendrocytes by proteolipid protein 1
distractor_notes: Dopamine synthesis defects do not produce the classic brief kinesigenic-triggered familial attacks with normal interictal examination.
GABA-transaminase abnormalities cause epileptic/developmental syndromes rather than PRRT2-related PKD.
Neuromuscular acetylcholine release abnormalities cause weakness, not central paroxysmal dyskinesia.
PLP1 dysfunction causes hypomyelinating leukodystrophy, not seconds-long movement-triggered attacks.
key_expl: PRRT2-related disorder is a presynaptic synaptic-transmission disorder. Paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia is characterized by very brief movement-triggered dyskinesias with preserved awareness and a normal examination between events.
objective: Connect classic paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia with PRRT2-dependent presynaptic neurotransmission.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Patient Care: Diagnosis, including history and physical examination
diagnosis: Alternating hemiplegia of childhood due to ATP1A3 dysfunction
mechanism: ATP1A3 encodes a neuronal Na+/K+-ATPase alpha subunit. Pathogenic variants can produce alternating hemiplegia of childhood, with onset before 18 months, recurrent hemiplegic or quadriplegic episodes, dystonia/abnormal eye movements, developmental abnormalities, and a characteristic improvement or remission of attacks during sleep.
vignette: A 14-month-old girl has recurrent episodes of weakness affecting either the right or left side of the body; some episodes progress to quadriplegia and dystonic posturing. Between episodes she has mild developmental delay and intermittent abnormal eye movements. The episodes often stop after she falls asleep and may recur shortly after awakening. Brain MRI is unrevealing.
lead: Which diagnosis best explains these findings?
distractors: Hemiplegic migraine
Todd paralysis after focal seizures
Moyamoya disease
Paroxysmal kinesigenic dyskinesia
distractor_notes: Hemiplegic migraine can cause episodic weakness but does not characteristically begin before 18 months with alternating/quadriplegic episodes and sleep-dependent remission plus developmental abnormalities.
Todd paralysis follows epileptic seizures and does not show the characteristic alternating pattern with sleep-dependent spell resolution.
Moyamoya causes ischemic events related to cerebrovascular stenosis and is not expected to resolve consistently with sleep.
PRRT2-related PKD produces seconds-long movement-triggered dyskinesia rather than prolonged hemiplegia relieved by sleep.
key_expl: Alternating hemiplegia of childhood is a classic ATP1A3-related phenotype. Onset is before 18 months, weakness alternates sides or becomes quadriplegic, developmental/oculomotor abnormalities occur, and spells characteristically improve with sleep.
objective: Recognize ATP1A3-related alternating hemiplegia of childhood from early onset, alternating hemiplegia, developmental abnormalities, and sleep-dependent spell remission.

system: Behavioral Health, Nervous Systems and Special Senses
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
mechanism: FOLR1 encodes folate receptor alpha at the choroid plexus. Loss of function impairs folate transport across the blood-choroid-plexus-CSF barrier, producing very low CSF folate despite normal systemic folate and later-onset developmental regression, seizures, movement abnormalities, and hypomyelination.
vignette: A 3-year-old girl who developed normally during infancy has progressive gait instability, tremor, seizures, and loss of previously acquired language. MRI shows cerebral hypomyelination. Hemoglobin, mean corpuscular volume, and serum folate are normal. Cerebrospinal fluid 5-methyltetrahydrofolate is markedly reduced. Genetic testing identifies biallelic FOLR1 pathogenic variants.
lead: Which transport process is primarily impaired?
correct: Folate transport across the choroid plexus into cerebrospinal fluid
distractors: Intestinal folate uptake across the apical enterocyte membrane
Cellular vitamin B12 uptake through intrinsic-factor receptors in the terminal ileum
Glucose transport across blood-brain-barrier endothelial cells
Tetrahydrobiopterin recycling within monoamine-producing neurons
distractor_notes: Primary intestinal folate malabsorption produces systemic folate deficiency and hematologic abnormalities, which are absent here.
Vitamin B12 uptake defects cause systemic cobalamin deficiency rather than isolated low CSF folate with FOLR1 variants.
GLUT1 deficiency causes low CSF glucose rather than very low CSF folate.
Tetrahydrobiopterin defects alter aromatic amino-acid hydroxylation and neurotransmitter synthesis, not selective choroid-plexus folate transport.
key_expl: FOLR1 loss causes cerebral folate transport deficiency by impairing folate-receptor-alpha-mediated movement of folate across the choroid plexus into CSF. Systemic folate status can remain normal, making the CSF-serum dissociation highly informative.
objective: Distinguish FOLR1 cerebral folate transport deficiency from systemic folate deficiency by recognizing very low CSF folate with normal serum folate and blood counts.
clues: normal serum folate and blood count
duplicate_probe_terms: folate receptor alpha choroid plexus CSF
